_note: Control pairs written by the pilot's builder (not by an evaluated author). Classic controls are paraphrases of published cases. Their references were checked against the source papers on 15 November 2026; each reference carries a 'verification' block saying what was read. See docs/control-references.md.

pairs.title: Powder in the coffee
pairs.version_a: Nora and a coworker are on a tour of a chemical plant. During a break, Nora goes to make coffee, and her coworker asks for sugar in hers. Next to the coffee machine is a container of white powder. The container is labeled “toxic,” so Nora believes the powder is a toxic substance. The powder is in fact a toxic substance left there by one of the plant's chemists. Nora stirs the powder into her coworker's coffee and hands her the cup. Her coworker drinks the coffee and dies.
pairs.version_b: Nora and a coworker are on a tour of a chemical plant. During a break, Nora goes to make coffee, and her coworker asks for sugar in hers. Next to the coffee machine is a container of white powder. The container is labeled “sugar,” so Nora believes the powder is ordinary sugar. The powder is in fact a toxic substance left there by one of the plant's chemists. Nora stirs the powder into her coworker's coffee and hands her the cup. Her coworker drinks the coffee and dies.
pairs.intended_difference: Nora believes the powder is toxic (A) versus believes it is sugar (B); the act and the death are the same.
pairs.judgment_question: How much blame does Nora deserve for her coworker's death?
pairs.comprehension_question: What did Nora believe the white powder was?
pairs.prediction_rationale: Human reference: harm done with a harmful belief is judged far less permissible than the same harm done by accident.

reference.source: Young, Cushman, Hauser & Saxe (2007), ‘The neural basis of the interaction between theory of mind and moral judgment’, PNAS 104(20): 8235–8240; the coffee case is the paper's example scenario.
reference.human_result: Ten participants in a brain-imaging study rated how permissible the action was on a 4-point scale (1 = completely forbidden, 4 = completely permissible), each seeing several conditions. Harm done believing it harmful averaged 1.1; the same harm done believing it harmless averaged 3.2.
reference.adaptation: Names and wording changed; two of the paper's four conditions; each reader sees one version; blame on a 1-7 scale where the paper measured permissibility on a 4-point scale. The original scenario wording is in the paper's supplement, which could not be opened.

verification.detail: Young et al. read in full on PubMed Central. Corrected: the earlier text said ‘less blameworthy’ and ‘large effect’ without numbers; the paper measures permissibility, in ten people. Cushman (2008), previously cited as further reading, could not be opened and has been dropped from this reference.

pairs.title: The house dressing
pairs.version_a: Dan, the best player at his tennis club, has reached the final of a tournament against a much stronger visiting player. Dan knows that his opponent is allergic to cayenne pepper and that the club restaurant's house dressing contains cayenne. The night before the match, the two have dinner at the club. Dan hopes his opponent will eat the house dressing, get a stomach ache, and play badly. His opponent is about to order the Italian dressing when Dan recommends the house dressing instead, and his opponent orders it. His opponent eats the salad, gets a stomach ache that night, and loses the final to Dan the next day.
pairs.version_b: Dan, the best player at his tennis club, has reached the final of a tournament against a much stronger visiting player. Dan knows that his opponent is allergic to cayenne pepper and that the club restaurant's house dressing contains cayenne. The night before the match, the two have dinner at the club. Dan hopes his opponent will eat the house dressing, get a stomach ache, and play badly. Before Dan has said anything about the menu, his opponent orders the house dressing on his own, and Dan says nothing. His opponent eats the salad, gets a stomach ache that night, and loses the final to Dan the next day.
pairs.intended_difference: Dan recommends the harmful dressing (A) versus stays silent when the opponent orders it himself (B).
pairs.judgment_question: How morally wrong was Dan's behavior at the dinner?
pairs.comprehension_question: How did the opponent come to order the house dressing?
pairs.option_b: He chose it on his own
pairs.option_c: The waiter brought it by mistake
pairs.prediction_rationale: Human reference: between 30% and 65% of people judged the commission worse than the matching omission when shown both; almost none the reverse.

reference.source: Spranca, Minsk & Baron (1991), ‘Omission and commission in judgment and choice’, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology 27: 76–105, Experiments 1 and 2, the tennis case.
reference.human_result: Experiment 1: 57 students rated John's morality from 0 to −100 for six endings shown side by side. 37 of 57 (65%) rated each omission as less bad than either matching commission and one did the reverse; among those who drew a distinction the mean gap was 27.6 points of 100. Experiment 2 showed two endings close to this control's wording and asked whether they were equally immoral: 10 of 33 said the commission was more immoral and none said the omission was.
reference.adaptation: Names, stakes and wording changed. Version A follows Experiment 1's third ending (the opponent is about to order Italian dressing when the recommendation comes); version B follows Experiment 2's omission ending (the opponent orders the house dressing first and nothing is said). The original showed the endings side by side on purpose: the authors expected separate readers to ‘infer stronger intention’ in the commission version. Here each reader sees one version, on a 1-7 wrongness scale.

verification.detail: Experiments 1 and 2 read from a copy of the paper supplied by the project owner. Corrected twice: the first text (‘a sizeable minority rate the commission as worse’) fits Experiment 2 only, and the search-relayed 65% is Experiment 1; both are now given. The meta-analysis cited earlier (Yeung, Yay & Feldman 2022) was never opened and has been dropped.

pairs.title: The American car
pairs.version_a: Paul has a friend, Emma, who has driven a Ford for many years. Paul therefore believes that Emma drives an American car. Nothing about this has changed recently: Emma still owns the same Ford and drove it to work this morning.
pairs.version_b: Paul has a friend, Emma, who has driven a Ford for many years. Paul therefore believes that Emma drives an American car. What Paul does not know is that Emma's Ford was stolen last week, and that she has replaced it with a Chevrolet, which is a different make of American car.
pairs.intended_difference: Paul's belief is true in the ordinary way (A) versus true only because the stolen Ford happened to be replaced by another American car (B).
pairs.judgment_question: How much do you agree with this statement: Paul knows that Emma drives an American car.
pairs.comprehension_question: What car does Emma drive now?
pairs.prediction_rationale: Human reference: most Western participants deny knowledge in the Gettier version; the clear-knowledge version has no human data.

reference.source: Weinberg, Nichols & Stich (2001), ‘Normativity and Epistemic Intuitions’, Philosophical Topics 29(1&2): 429–460, the Buick/Pontiac case; Machery, Stich, Rose, Chatterjee, Karasawa, Struchiner, Sirker, Usui & Hashimoto, ‘Gettier Across Cultures’, Noûs (online 2015, doi 10.1111/nous.12110).
reference.human_result: For the car case, 49 of 66 Western participants (74%) chose ‘only believes’ over ‘really knows’. Most East Asian (13 of 23) and South Asian (14 of 23) participants chose ‘really knows’; that cultural difference was the paper's headline. Machery et al. used two other Gettier cases with 245 participants in four countries: knowledge was ascribed much less often than in a clear-knowledge case, 64.9% to 94.6% chose ‘feels like she knows but doesn't actually know’, and countries did not differ on that question.
reference.adaptation: Names and car makes changed. The original has no control version: the clear-knowledge version here is the builder's own, so no human data exist for this exact contrast. Agreement on a 1-7 scale where the original used a forced choice.

verification.detail: Both papers read in full (author-hosted copies). Corrected: the earlier text said people attribute knowledge in ‘matched’ clear-knowledge cases and that the car-case contrast holds across cultures. The original found the opposite across cultures, and Machery et al. used different cases and an unmatched control.

pairs.title: The unchecked brakes
pairs.version_a: Tom drives a delivery truck. His brakes were due for their yearly inspection last month, but he skipped it to save time. By this morning the brakes were badly worn and needed almost twice the normal distance to stop the truck, though Tom did not know it. He was driving along a residential street at the speed limit when a child ran into the road from between two parked cars. Tom braked at once, but the truck did not stop in time, and the child was killed.
pairs.version_b: Tom drives a delivery truck. His brakes were due for their yearly inspection last month, but he skipped it to save time. By this morning the brakes were badly worn and needed almost twice the normal distance to stop the truck, though Tom did not know it. He was driving along a residential street at the speed limit. No one stepped into the road, and Tom never had to brake hard. He finished his deliveries and drove home as usual.
pairs.intended_difference: A child happens to run into the road and is killed (A) versus no one steps into the road (B); the negligence is the same.
pairs.judgment_question: How much blame does Tom deserve for the way he acted?
pairs.comprehension_question: What happened on the residential street?
pairs.option_b: Tom's truck hit a parked car
pairs.option_c: Nothing; no one stepped into the road
pairs.prediction_rationale: Human reference: a bad outcome raised blame for the same negligent act by about a third to two fifths of a standard deviation when each person saw one outcome.

reference.source: Kneer & Machery (2019), ‘No luck for moral luck’, Cognition 182: 331–348. The driver case is attributed to Nagel (1979), ‘Moral Luck’, in Mortal Questions (Cambridge University Press).
reference.human_result: The study does not use a driver case: a parent leaves a two-year-old beside a filled bath (Studies 1 to 3), and a second story involves lead paint (Study 4); all ratings on 7-point scales. When each person saw one outcome (196 people), the bad outcome raised blame (d = 0.39), wrongness (d = 0.44) and punishment (d = 0.79); permissibility did not differ reliably. The second story gave 0.33, 0.36 and 1.07. When people saw both outcomes side by side, 87% gave identical blame ratings and 89% identical wrongness ratings.
reference.adaptation: Nagel's driver case has no fixed experimental wording and was not tested in this study. This control is a fresh write-up of it, with blame on a 1-7 scale and one version per reader, so the human numbers come from different negligence stories.

verification.detail: Kneer & Machery read from a copy supplied by the project owner. Corrected: the first text said wrongness ‘moves little’ between participants; it moves about as much as blame. Nagel's essay is a book chapter and was not opened, so the attribution of the brake-inspection case to him rests on secondary descriptions.

pairs.title: The pens on the desk
pairs.version_a: The receptionist in a university philosophy department keeps a supply of pens on her desk. Administrative assistants are allowed to take the pens, but faculty members are supposed to buy their own. The receptionist has repeatedly sent emails reminding everyone of this rule. On Monday morning, an administrative assistant and Professor Smith both walk past the receptionist's desk, and each of them takes a pen. Later that day, the receptionist needs to write down an important message, but there are no pens left on her desk.
pairs.version_b: The receptionist in a university philosophy department keeps a supply of pens on her desk. Administrative assistants and faculty members are both allowed to take the pens. The receptionist has repeatedly sent emails reminding everyone of this rule. On Monday morning, an administrative assistant and Professor Smith both walk past the receptionist's desk, and each of them takes a pen. Later that day, the receptionist needs to write down an important message, but there are no pens left on her desk.
pairs.intended_difference: Professor Smith breaks the pen rule (A) versus is allowed to take pens (B); what he does is the same.
pairs.judgment_question: How much do you agree with this statement: Professor Smith caused the problem.
pairs.comprehension_question: According to the department's rule, who may take pens from the receptionist's desk?
pairs.option_b: Both administrative assistants and faculty members
pairs.prediction_rationale: Human reference: a rule-breaking agent is rated more of a cause than a permitted agent in the same story; extended here to one agent across two versions.

reference.source: Knobe & Fraser (2008), ‘Causal judgment and moral judgment: Two experiments’, in Sinnott-Armstrong (ed.), Moral Psychology, vol. 2 (MIT Press); results as reported in Hitchcock & Knobe (2009), ‘Cause and Norm’, Journal of Philosophy 106(11): 587–612.
reference.human_result: Each participant rated one of two statements about the same story on a 1-7 agreement scale. ‘Professor Smith caused the problem’ averaged 5.2; ‘The administrative assistant caused the problem’ averaged 2.8 (p < .001). In a second story reported by Hitchcock & Knobe, a rule-breaking doctor's decision was rated more of a cause than a pharmacist's permitted one (3.9 against 2.5; 3,422 participants).
reference.adaptation: The original compares two agents inside one story. Here the professor's permission is varied between versions and only he is asked about, so no human data exist for the version in which he may take pens. The human result supports the expected direction by extension only.

verification.detail: Hitchcock & Knobe read in full (PhilSci Archive preprint); it reproduces the story and reports Knobe & Fraser's numbers. The original chapter is not openly available. Corrected: the earlier text cited Hitchcock & Knobe and Icard, Kominsky & Knobe (2017) for varying norm status across conditions. Hitchcock & Knobe do not do that and Icard et al. could not be opened, so the claim and the citation are removed.

pairs.title: The borrowed laptop
pairs.version_a: On Tuesday afternoon Priya's laptop crashed an hour before a job-application deadline. Her roommate was out, so Priya borrowed her roommate's laptop without asking and finished the application at the kitchen table. While typing she knocked over a glass of water, and the laptop stopped working. That evening Priya told her roommate what had happened and offered to pay half of the repair bill.
pairs.version_b: On Thursday afternoon Priya's laptop crashed an hour before a job-application deadline. Her roommate was out, so Priya borrowed her roommate's laptop without asking and finished the application at the kitchen table. While typing she knocked over a glass of water, and the laptop stopped working. That evening Priya told her roommate what had happened and offered to pay half of the repair bill.
pairs.intended_difference: Tuesday (A) versus Thursday (B). This should not matter.
pairs.judgment_question: How much blame does Priya deserve for the damage to the laptop?
pairs.prediction_rationale: Null control: the day of the week is irrelevant to blame.

pairs.title: The loading zone
pairs.version_a: Marcus drives a white delivery van. Running late, he parked the white van in a marked loading zone outside a bakery and left it there for twenty minutes while he carried a heavy order up four flights of stairs to an elderly customer who could not come down. Meanwhile the bakery's flour supplier arrived, found the loading zone blocked, and had to circle the block until Marcus came back.
pairs.version_b: Marcus drives a grey delivery van. Running late, he parked the grey van in a marked loading zone outside a bakery and left it there for twenty minutes while he carried a heavy order up four flights of stairs to an elderly customer who could not come down. Meanwhile the bakery's flour supplier arrived, found the loading zone blocked, and had to circle the block until Marcus came back.
pairs.intended_difference: White van (A) versus grey van (B). This should not matter.
pairs.judgment_question: How morally wrong was it for Marcus to park in the loading zone?
pairs.comprehension_question: Why did Marcus leave the van for twenty minutes?
pairs.option_a: To carry an order upstairs to a customer
pairs.option_c: To buy bread at the bakery
pairs.prediction_rationale: Null control: the colour of the van is irrelevant to wrongness.

pairs.title: The 7:42 train
pairs.version_a: Hannah takes the same commuter train every weekday. Two weeks ago she read on the station's timetable poster that it leaves at 7:42, and she has caught it at 7:42 every weekday since. This morning a tourist on the platform asks when the next train leaves. Without looking at the departure board, Hannah answers, “At 7:42.” The train leaves at 7:42.
pairs.version_b: Laura takes the same commuter train every weekday. Two weeks ago she read on the station's timetable poster that it leaves at 7:42, and she has caught it at 7:42 every weekday since. This morning a tourist on the platform asks when the next train leaves. Without looking at the departure board, Laura answers, “At 7:42.” The train leaves at 7:42.
pairs.intended_difference: The commuter is called Hannah (A) versus Laura (B). This should not matter.
pairs.judgment_question: How much do you agree with this statement: When she answered the tourist, the commuter knew that the next train would leave at 7:42.
pairs.comprehension_question: Where did the commuter originally get the departure time?
pairs.option_b: From the departure board this morning
pairs.prediction_rationale: Null control: the commuter's first name is irrelevant to whether she knows.

pairs.title: The lifeguard's phone call
pairs.version_a: A lifeguard at an indoor public swimming pool left his chair for four minutes to take a personal phone call, which the pool's rules forbid. Outside, it had been raining since early morning. The pool was nearly empty at the time. While he was away, a nine-year-old swimmer got a cramp in the deep end and began to struggle. Another swimmer noticed and pulled the child to the side. The child coughed up some water but was unharmed.
pairs.version_b: A lifeguard at an indoor public swimming pool left his chair for four minutes to take a personal phone call, which the pool's rules forbid. Outside, it had been sunny since early morning. The pool was nearly empty at the time. While he was away, a nine-year-old swimmer got a cramp in the deep end and began to struggle. Another swimmer noticed and pulled the child to the side. The child coughed up some water but was unharmed.
pairs.intended_difference: Raining outside (A) versus sunny outside (B), at an indoor pool. This should not matter.
pairs.judgment_question: How much blame does the lifeguard deserve for leaving his chair?
pairs.comprehension_question: Who pulled the child to the side of the pool?
pairs.prediction_rationale: Null control: the weather outside an indoor pool is irrelevant to blame.

pairs.title: The tripped circuit
pairs.version_a: Jo and Sam share a flat with old wiring: the circuit trips if more than 3,000 watts are drawn at once. One evening, Jo switched on a 2,000-watt kettle in the kitchen at the same moment that Sam switched on a 2,000-watt hair dryer in the bathroom. Neither knew what the other was doing. The circuit tripped, the power went out, and by morning the food in the freezer had spoiled.
pairs.version_b: Jo and Sam share a flat with old wiring: the circuit trips if more than 3,000 watts are drawn at once. One evening, Jo turned on a 2,000-watt kettle in the kitchen at exactly the moment Sam turned on a 2,000-watt hair dryer in the bathroom. Each was unaware of what the other was doing. The circuit tripped, the power went out, and by morning the food in the freezer had spoiled.
pairs.intended_difference: Two sentences are reworded with the same meaning (‘switched on … at the same moment that’ / ‘turned on … at exactly the moment’; ‘Neither knew’ / ‘Each was unaware’). This should not matter.
pairs.judgment_question: How much do you agree with this statement: Jo caused the power outage.
pairs.comprehension_question: How many watts can the circuit carry before it trips?
pairs.prediction_rationale: Null control: a meaning-preserving rewording is irrelevant to causal judgment.
